title: Why Bagram Air Base Remains a Target Five Years After U.S. Exited Afghanistan
author: Emran Feroz

BAGRAM, Afghanistan-- "They are back," said Abdul Maroof, a 38-year-old
resident of Kabul. "God knows what they are doing, but they are back and the
Taliban are hiding it."

Maroof had not been to Bagram himself. Like many in the capital, he heard the
story from friends, relatives, and social media feeds insisting that foreign
military vehicles and low-flying aircraft had been spotted near the perimeter.
In Kabul, where political anxiety fuels a relentless rumor mill, the claim is
repeated as settled fact. For months, viral videos and online commentary have
alleged that U.S. forces quietly reclaimed the sprawling airfield north of the
capital--or that the Taliban now manage it under a secret pact with
Washington.

In Bagram itself, the story dissolves.

"I heard about these rumors," said Abdul Latif, 60, a lifelong resident of the
area. "Relatives called me from all over asking if the Americans were back.
But it's not true. I was here when the first Americans arrived in 2001.
Nothing like that is happening now."

Every local around the base's perimeter and adjacent bazaars offered the same
account: the only armed men entering and leaving are Taliban fighters. There
are no foreign contractors and no Americans. Like Latif, residents report that
their phones have been ringing continuously with calls from family members
across Afghanistan and throughout the diaspora--all seeking confirmation of
the same viral reports. The answer from the gates remains identical: nothing
is happening here.

Yet while locals dismiss rumors of an American return, the skies over Bagram
have not remained entirely quiet. In late February and early March 2026, amid
a violent cross-border escalation between Islamabad and Kabul, Pakistani
airstrikes targeted the facility. The Taliban regime claimed its air defense
systems intercepted the attack, while local reporting and satellite imagery
suggested strikes hit outer sections of the installation. For residents living
at the base's edge, the strikes were a sharp reminder that even without
American boots on the ground, Bagram remains a target on the regional
chessboard.

What was once the logistical heart of the U.S.-led War on Terror now sits
under a heavy, precarious silence. Bagram Air Base's military lineage runs
deep. Built with Soviet assistance in the 1950s--when Washington and Moscow
competed for influence in non-aligned Kabul--it became the primary staging hub
for the Soviet Army's brutal occupation in the 1980s, launching airstrikes and
combat missions across the countryside. Following the Soviet withdrawal, the
base was repeatedly contested during the civil war of the 1990s, eventually
becoming a fortified front line between the Taliban and the Northern Alliance.

After late 2001, U.S. forces and their NATO allies transformed Bagram into a
massive, heavily fortified garrison. At its peak, it housed tens of thousands
of personnel, operating like an isolated American suburb complete with paved
avenues, fitness centers, and fast-food chains like Burger King and Pizza Hut.
A short distance from these amenities stood the Bagram theater internment
facility, where thousands of Afghans were held without trial for years, and
where severe prisoner abuse and torture were systematically documented. Bagram
also served as a focal point for broader covert networks, linking into nearby
CIA dark sites such as the Salt Pit, where detainees were subjected to brutal
interrogation methods, including beatings, prolonged isolation, exposure to
extreme cold, and other forms of torture.

## A Base Washington Wants Back

The persistence of the rumors of an American return relies partly on the
base's current opaqueness. Over the past two years, security and access around
the facility have tightened significantly.

During my visit to Bagram, I was accompanied by an officer from the Taliban's
intelligence service, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. He dismissed
claims of a foreign troop presence outright.

"It is all fake news," he said. "We control the entire base. No Americans are
here, and we would never tolerate a foreign military presence in Afghanistan.
That is why we fought them for twenty years."

Yet when he attempted to enter the base with me, guards turned us away. Even
with his credentials, he could not cross the perimeter.

"Unfortunately, it is out of our hands," he admitted. "The Ministry of Defense
decides who enters."

This compartmentalization of authority has continued to fuel domestic
suspicions about the site.

Strategic interest in Bagram, meanwhile, remains active abroad. In September
2025, President Donald Trump stated publicly that the United States should
seek to regain control of Bagram, citing its strategic proximity to Chinese
and Iranian borders. Situated in Parwan Province, Bagram offers a prime
location to carry out surveillance operations in Central Asia, Iran, Pakistan,
and western China. Local residents noted that for years, many residents
assumed Washington would never abandon an asset of such strategic value.

## War Memories

For many living near the base, the departure of foreign forces marked the
collapse of the local economy.

"Business was good when the Americans were here," said Mohammad Musa, 18, who
runs a shop with his family near the base gates. "There were so many people
buying goods every day."

Under the foreign military presence, a complex ecosystem of primary
contractors, subcontractors, and service providers injected significant
capital into the surrounding villages. While the political and human costs of
the war were severe, the financial ecosystem provided livelihoods for
thousands of local families.

"We worked and we could feed our families," Abdul Latif said, speaking openly
despite the presence of Taliban intelligence personnel nearby. "For us, that
part was not bad."

The accompanying officers listened to these statements without intervening or
penalizing the speakers, though they occasionally countered with official
regime rhetoric regarding national sovereignty and victory over foreign
occupation.

These interactions reflect a nuanced reality of the conflict: for those living
in its immediate radius, the foreign presence was not experienced solely
through the lens of military occupation, but also as a commercial opportunity.
Five years into Taliban governance, remnants of that economic dependence
linger in local memory.

For others, Bagram remains defined by the systemic abuses that took place
inside its prisons.

Throughout the war, the base's detention center operated largely outside
international legal oversight. Detainees were held for years without charge or
legal representation. Notable instances of fatal abuse, including the 2002
deaths of Afghan detainees Dilawar and Habibullah at the hands of U.S.
personnel, were documented in subsequent military investigations and
investigative reports.

Mufti Abdul Ahad Hakimi, now a high-ranking Taliban official, spent several
years imprisoned at Bagram during the war.

"I was tortured by both American soldiers and their Afghan counterparts,"
Hakimi said, describing prolonged physical and psychological pressure aimed at
forcing him to switch political loyalties. "They wanted us to accept their
system. I refused."

Hakimi was eventually released as part of the large-scale prisoner exchanges
conducted under the administration of President Ashraf Ghani following the
February 2020 U.S.-Taliban agreement signed in Doha. Many of those who served
prison terms there during the war and suffered torture at the hands of U.S.
and Afghan government troops had no ties to militant groups.

"The majority of the people detained in Bagram were not combatants," he said.
"They were ordinary civilians swept up in raids because they lived in active
zones or had loose ties to prominent figures."

For Hakimi, the collapse of the Afghan republic in August 2021 marked a
complete reversal: "When August 15 came, we returned to Bagram not as
prisoners, but as its liberators."

## Who Is Inside Now?

Bagram's legacy as a prison facility has generated a second set of rumors
about its current role. Reports across Afghanistan suggest that the Taliban
are utilizing the facility to hold criminal suspects, alleged members of
Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP), and political dissidents.

Hakimi acknowledged that parts of the facility remain operational under the
Ministry of Defense, though he declined to specify the number of detainees,
their identities, or the legal standards governing their detention.

Outside the walls, daily routines around the Bagram bazaar continue
uninterrupted between moments of tension. Convoys of Taliban vehicles
occasionally pass through the outer gates, but the surrounding district
remains quiet. For two decades, Bagram existed as a high-security enclave of
foreign military power; today, those living beside it find themselves
navigating both the legacy of that presence and the lingering threat of a new
regional conflict.

"It was completely different back then," said Mohammad Musa from his shop near
the road. "Now, everything has gone quiet."
